vignette:
Sunita is a 47-year-old pastor at a small South Asian Christian congregation in a Midwestern city. She came to this country seven years ago. She does not speak about what happened before that, not even to her closest deacons. But the story lives inside her, repeating in fragments that she cannot control.

She was a pastor in her home country, too—a woman leading a church in a city where religious minorities were increasingly targeted. She had been outspoken about the disappearances of young men from her community, writing letters to local newspapers, praying publicly for their safe return. One evening, she was pulled from her car at a checkpoint. Three men in civilian clothes forced her into the back of a van. They took her to a windowless room, and for fourteen days they asked her questions about her “affiliations” and her “network.” She told them the truth: she was only a pastor. They did not believe her.

The torture was systematic. They used electricity, beatings with rubber hoses, and submerging her head in water until she stopped struggling. They burned her arms with cigarettes. On the fifth day, she stopped counting. On the ninth, she tried to pray but could not find words. She felt God had left the room. On the fourteenth day, they dumped her near a hospital. She was never charged. She never saw them again.

After her release, she fled to a neighboring country and then was sponsored by a church in the United States. Her husband, also a pastor, stayed behind. He could not understand why she could not “move on.” He accused her of being cold, distant, broken. After two years of long-distance attempts, she filed for divorce. She has not remarried. She rarely speaks of him.

Now, in her small rented apartment, Sunita wakes most nights at 3:00 a.m. with her heart pounding, certain she hears footsteps in the hallway. She always checks the locks before bed, sometimes three or four times. She no longer answers the door without a peephole check. At the grocery store, she stands with her back to the wall, scanning the aisles. She avoids crowded places and asks her assistant to handle all evening meetings.

Her pastoral work suffers in quieter ways. She preaches with her notes close at hand, unable to trust her memory. She no longer leads the prayer chain because the phone calls feel like surveillance. When a young woman in the congregation confides that she is being threatened by a former partner, Sunita listens but does not touch her hand. Physical contact makes her flinch. She feels shame about this—she is supposed to be a healer, not a wounded person who cannot help.

On Sunday mornings, she stands in the pulpit and sees the faces of the three men. They blend into the back pews. She blinks and they are gone. She carries a small cloth in her pocket, worn smooth from rubbing between her fingers during the sermon. It helps, barely.

She cannot pray the way she used to. Words feel hollow. She reads Scripture and feels only a cold distance. She believes God failed her, and this belief scares her more than the nightmares. She has not said it aloud to anyone.

The PCL-5 score of 53 reflects what she lives every day: hypervigilance, avoidance, intrusive memories, negative alterations in mood, and a shrinking world. But in session, she does not use these words. She says, “I am tired.” She says, “I don’t know who I am anymore.” She says, “I do not want to be a pastor but I do not know how to be anything else.”
